query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning-based process–structure–property model, integrating thermodynamic and kinetic data from Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, can provide a systematic way to predict and thereby control phase evolution under different processing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy samples with nominally equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition.
generation.intervention: Implementing data-driven modeling (e.g., machine learning with CALPHAD-based thermodynamic and kinetic inputs) to guide and refine heat-treatment schedules.
generation.conditions: Varying the aging/annealing temperatures and times in a targeted manner, based on model predictions, to favor specific intermetallic precipitation or phase stability pathways.
generation.structural_mediator: The competition between refined B2, disordered BCC, and potential FCC phases, controlled by temperature–time processing profiles predicted by the model.
generation.mechanism: The model unifies scattered experimental data and thermodynamic calculations to estimate how different compositions and thermal histories shift the relative stability of competing phases, enabling a feedback loop of iterative processing adjustments.
generation.predicted_outcome: A shorter, systematic route to achieving stable or metastable microstructures optimized for desired mechanical or physical properties in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
generation.baseline: Empirical trial-and-error or purely theoretical predictions without iterative data-driven guidance, which are more time-intensive and less robust.
generation.boundary: Method performance depends on the availability of accurate thermodynamic and kinetic databases for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni, and predictions should be experimentally validated for compositional ranges with limited prior data.
generation.uncertainty: While initial simulation and experimental results are encouraging, the accuracy of predictions relies on the coverage and fidelity of training data and may need correction and recalibration for new compositions or extreme processing conditions.

cited_evidence.text: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. Here, we propose a highly efficient DFT-based method aided by a specially designed machine learning potential. As the machine learning potential can closely reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, even for multi-component alloys, the costly thermodynamic integration can be fully substituted with more efficient free energy perturbation calculations. The method achieves overall savings of computational resources by 80% compared to current alternatives. We apply the method to the high-entropy alloy TaVCrW and calculate its melting properties

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

decision.trend: Early work (2016, PMC4999872) on AlxCoCrFeNi HEAs focused on how single-phase vs. multiphase structures respond to external stimuli such as ion irradiation, revealing that precipitation behavior differs sharply between the two. In 2019 (PMC7515071), powder metallurgy (gas atomization plus spark plasma sintering) was employed in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 to refine the microstructure and improve wear resistance, indicating that carefully tuned processing can alter phase assemblages. More recently (2025, PMC12806431), detailed isothermal aging studies of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 exposed how delicate changes in temperature can cause tempering-like embrittlement or restore ductility, underscoring how complex multiphase equilibria necessitate further methods to predict and control transformations. Despite these advances, a direct, predictive framework to guide phase control in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs—without protracted trial-and-error—remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: A robust, data-driven method to accurately predict how processing conditions (time–temperature history) govern phase stability and transformations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs has not yet been established. Researchers still lack a consistent, scalable approach for anticipating and steering multiphase microstructures toward optimal performance.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning-based process–structure–property model that integrates thermodynamic and kinetic data for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni. Use existing databases (calibrated against experiment) to rapidly screen aging/annealing schedules and predict phase stability pathways.
decision.why: Given the demonstrated sensitivity of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA phase evolution to subtle changes in processing history, a data-driven machine-learning approach can unify scattered experimental findings and thermodynamic models. This strategy enables systematic, predictive screening of time–temperature conditions, accelerating the identification of optimal processing paths for targeted multiphase control.
